title: References: Copies, Aliases, and the Angle Bug

questions.question: A function takes Pose p by value and sets p.x to zero. What does the caller see?
options: A compile error
The caller's pose is left uninitialised
Nothing changed, because the function modified a copy
The caller's pose has x set to zero
questions.explanation: Passing by value copies the argument. The function changes its own copy, which is discarded when it returns.

questions.question: What does const Pose& mean as a parameter type?
options: A pointer that may be null
An alias to the caller's object that the function is not allowed to change
A reference that is copied only if it is modified
A copy that cannot be changed
questions.explanation: The ampersand avoids the copy and const stops the function modifying it, which is the default choice for read only struct parameters.

questions.question: Why is the shortest turn from 179 degrees to minus 179 degrees only two degrees?
options: Because the robot can only turn anticlockwise
Because negative angles are measured differently
Because 179 and minus 179 are the same number
Because headings wrap, so the two directions are almost the same way round
questions.explanation: A full turn brings you back to where you started, so the useful answer is the smaller of the two ways round, which is two degrees.

questions.question: Why does the fmod version of wrap_angle need an extra check for negative results?
options: fmod keeps the sign of its left operand, so a negative input gives a negative remainder
To avoid dividing by zero
Because pi is irrational
fmod cannot accept negative numbers at all
questions.explanation: fmod truncates towards zero rather than wrapping, so negative inputs land outside the intended range and need one more turn added.

questions.question: When should a function take a plain reference rather than a const reference?
options: Only when the argument might be null
Whenever the argument is larger than eight bytes
Never, const references are always correct
When it is meant to modify the caller's object, and its name says so
questions.explanation: A non const reference is how a function changes the caller's data. The name should make that obvious, as in steer_towards or normalize_in_place.

questions.question: Why do three dimensional robotics libraries use quaternions instead of raw angles?
options: Because angles cannot be stored as doubles
Wrapping and gimbal lock make three separate angles unreliable to combine
Because ROS 2 does not support angles
Quaternions are faster to compute
questions.explanation: Composing rotations from three angles has singularities and wrap problems. Phase 06 builds quaternions from nothing and shows what they solve.
